Anthropic released Sonnet 5.5 today, and the model has an identity problem. Opus got cheaper, Fable arrived above both, and when we reviewed Sonnet 5 in July, we couldn’t find a task it handled best.

After a week of testing, we found its job. At low and medium effort, Sonnet 5.5 is fast, inexpensive, and responsive to direction, which makes it a strong partner for brainstorming, prototyping, and design work you steer yourself. Push it to high effort or leave it unattended, and it overbuilds.

We get into all of it in our Vibe Check https://every.?ev_audience=free, including:

Hi there,

On Friday, October 2 at 12 ET, I’m running AI Foundations: Prompting Is a Thinking Skill, a 60-minute workshop included with a paid Every subscription. We'll plan your week with an AI tool, and along the way I'll show you when a plain request is enough, what to explain when it isn't, and how to tell whether the answer is any good.

Subscribe and reserve your place ( https://0ab9ee3d.click.kit-mail3.com/92ul5d89lmhnh68ovepc9hz0gnp87uwh0gkeg/owhkhqhw0wxdwosvhr/aHR0cHM6Ly9ldmVyeS50by9ldmVudHMvcHJvbXB0aW5nLWlzLWEtdGhpbmtpbmctc2tpbGw_dXRtX3NvdXJjZT1raXQmdXRtX21lZGl1bT1lbWFpbCZ1dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249cHJvbXB0aW5nLXRoaW5raW5nLXNraWxsLW9jdDItYW5ub3VuY2UtZnJlZSZ1dG1fY29udGVudD1jdGEtYnV0dG9u )

Here’s why I built it:

Have you ever thought, “I could’ve done this myself by now”?

If you’ve spent 20 minutes trying to get AI to do something you thought would take two, you know the feeling. You explain it again. The next answer is longer, but still no closer to what you need. Eventually you do it yourself, and the next time you’re less likely to bother asking.

We spend a lot of time using this stuff and still get those answers. This workshop is about what to do with them. Bring an AI chat tool you can use; sharing is optional, and no coding experience or previous workshop is required. If you're not a paid subscriber yet, subscribing gets you a seat Friday, and at the rest of our live workshops too.

newsletters.content:
Can Microsoft make workplace agents useful at scale?  ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌ ‌

COPILOT GETS A SEAT IN THE ORG CHART https://every.?ev_audience=free


CAN MICROSOFT MAKE WORKPLACE AGENTS USEFUL AT SCALE? https://every.?ev_audience=free

by Ryan Sloan https://every.?ev_audience=free

Midjourney/Every illustration.

Was this newsletter forwarded to you? Sign up https://every.?ev_audience=free to get it in your inbox.



----------------------------------------



In August, Mike Taylor https://every.?ev_audience=free counted https://every.?ev_audience=free 80 Microsoft products called “Copilot.” Among them, he said, were some of the best tools for building agents—if you could navigate onboarding and enterprise IT administration.

On Wednesday, at a launch event in Redmond where I spoke with executives and briefly tried the app on the demo floor, Microsoft announced a new Copilot that combines chat, code, Office, and a persistent agent called Autopilot, replacing its separate consumer and work chat apps. Microsoft isn’t alone in attempting a unified interface for AI work https://every.?ev_audience=free, but its advantage is that the people it’s built for already spend their day in Outlook and Teams, with permissions their IT department set years ago.

Autopilot may be the most interesting piece of the new Copilot: It can work on its own and access most of what you can. Those permissions could make it useful and trustworthy inside a company, but they could also prevent it from completing an ordinary task. Microsoft’s own emphasis on evaluations (evals) at the launch event suggests that it is looking to its customers to define what good work looks like in their organizations and test whether Autopilot improves on current workflows.

 * Home brings chat, delegated tasks, and Word, Excel,

In today’s Context Window, we review Grok 4.7 (“a step backward”?) and explain why evals are suddenly everywhere. Elsewhere, head of social media Becky Isjwara breaks down her workflow for turning Every articles into viral short videos, head of platform Willie Williams https://every.?ev_audience=free argues that Slack agents are the new websites, and we share a fresh crop of Thesis Statements, including entries from Cmpnd’s Drew Breunig, Notion’s Geoffrey Litt, and MIT’s Daniela Rus, about what happens after automation.

MINI-VIBE CHECK

GROK 4.7 IS UNEVEN

Grok 4.7 launched publicly on Monday https://every.?ev_audience=free. And the vibes? Well, they are evolving.

In the team’s early tests, which began before the public release, the model was practically unusable. It left tasks unfinished, ignored instructions, and merged code without permission.

Every has numerous Grok 4.6 power users—notably Cora https://every.to/emails/click/1eb47536f45a3508ca723b5b2cb780e942839f966e324ef3162cd49469aec49f/eyJzdWJqZWN0IjoiV2h5IEV2YWxzIEFyZSBTbyBIb3QgUmlnaHQgTm93IiwicG9zdF9pZCI6NDQ5NCwicG9zdF90eXBlIjoicG9zdCIsInVybCI6Imh0dHBzOi8vY29yYS5jb21wdXRlci8_
